{{Short description|American chemist (1920 to 1974)}}
{{refimprove|date=September 2024}}
'''Ellis Ridgeway Lippincott Jr.''' (July 6, 1920 – December 24, 1974) was an American chemist, educator, inventor, science leader, and pioneer in spectroscopy. He was a professor of chemistry at the [[University of Maryland]] from 1955-1974 and served as director of the Center for Materials Research. According to ''[[Spectroscopy (magazine)|Spectroscopy]]'', Lippincott was an "icon of spectroscopy" and "one of the most influential [[spectroscopist]]s of the past 100 years."<ref name="Spectroscopy 2024">{{Cite journal |last=Workman |first=Jr |date=2024-07-01 |title=Ellis Ridgeway Lippincott: A Legacy of Scientific Innovation |url=https://www.spectroscopyonline.com/view/ellis-ridgeway-lippincott-a-legacy-of-scientific-innovation |journal=[[Spectroscopy (magazine)|Spectroscopy]] |series=June–July 2024 |language=en |volume=39 |issue=5 |pages=40–44|doi=10.56530/spectroscopy.ky8184w3 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Lippincott was born in [[Philadelphia]], [[Pennsylvania]] in 1920. A descendant of the earliest Quaker settlers of Pennsylvania and [[New Jersey]], he was raised in [[Medford, New Jersey|Medford]] and received his primary and secondary education at Moorestown Friends School in New Jersey.<ref>Moorestown Friends School Yearbook, The Cupola, 1939.</ref>{{fact|date=September 2024}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie L. |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--The Making of a Scientist |date=May 15, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-11-1 |pages=7–129 |language=en}}</ref>

Lippincott received his undergraduate degree from Earlham College in [[Richmond, Indiana]] in 1943. He received a master's degree from Johns Hopkins University followed by a Ph.D. from there in 1947. Afterward he spent a year doing post-doctoral work at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Spectroscopy Laboratory under lab director [[Richard C. Lord]], with whom he maintained a lifelong professional association.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie L. |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--The Making of a Scientist |date=May 15, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-11-1 |edition=1st |language=en}}</ref>

== Science career ==

Lippincott began his university teaching career as an Instructor of Chemistry at the [[University of Connecticut]] from 1948 to 1951. From 1951 to 1955, he was an associate professor of chemistry at [[Kansas State College]] in Manhattan, Kansas. In 1955, he became a professor of chemistry at the University of Maryland. At age 35, he was recognized as "one of the nation's top authorities on infrared and Raman [[spectroscopy]]."<ref>The Evening Sun of Baltimore, September 2, 1955, at 13.</ref> Lippincott remained at the University of Maryland until he died in 1974.

Lippincott was a frequent lecturer at scientific conferences, including [[Gordon Research Conferences]] and international conferences on spectroscopy, hydrogen bonding, and other scientific topics. He was program chair for the 10th Annual International Spectroscopy Colloquium in 1962 attended by 1,000 scientists from all over the world. He was a lecturer in the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Visiting Scientist Program.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--Lectures and Talks |date=May 15, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-10-4 |edition=1st |pages=135–180 |language=en}}</ref>

Lippincott was a regular faculty member of the summer Spectroscopy Course hosted by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Spectroscopy Laboratory, lecturing every year from 1956 onward.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mayo |first1=Dana W. |last2=Miller |first2=Foil A. |last3=Hannah |first3=Robert W. |title=Course Notes on the Interpretation of Infrared and Raman Spectra |date=2004 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=0471248231 |pages=front matter |language=en}}</ref>

He founded and directed the Laser Raman Institute and Workshop at the University of Maryland, a week-long training program for scientists in the application of laser methods of research and featuring lectures by distinguished scientists on the theory of Raman spectroscopy and interpretation of spectra and instruction in advanced instrumentation.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie L. |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--Research Grants |date=May 15, 2024 |isbn=978-1-963587-04-3 |pages=171–200}}</ref>

In 1968, he founded the ''Raman Newsletter'', a monthly newsletter he edited as a clearinghouse for current developments in experiments and research in Raman spectroscopy.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie L. |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--Professional Activities |date=May 15, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-08-1 |pages=119–208 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Center for Materials Research ===
Much of Lippincott's research was interdisciplinary in the field of materials science. He was instrumental in creating the Center for Materials Research at the University of Maryland and served as its director from 1967 to 1974. The center was one of 12 elite interdisciplinary laboratories sponsored by the Advanced Projects Research Agency (predecessor to the Defense Department's [[DARPA]]). As director, Lippincott was responsible for the scientific management of the Center and its research output.

=== Research ===
Lippincott's scientific research spanned a wide range of areas, including [[physical chemistry]], [[quantum chemistry]], biophysics, molecular spectra and structure, high-pressure optics, [[thermodynamic equilibrium]] in complex systems, infrared and [[Raman spectroscopy]], hydrogen bonding, potential energy functions, applications of spectral studies to biochemistry and chemical applications of [[laser]]s, chemical and analytical applications of induced electron emission spectroscopy.

Much of Lippincott's scientific research was funded by the Advanced Projects Research Agency, [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]], [[NASA|National Aeronautics and Space Administration]], [[National Science Foundation]], [[Army Research Office]], and [[United States Public Health Service|Public Health Service]].{{fact|date=September 2024}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie L. |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--Research Grants |date=May 15, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-04-3 |pages=1–554 |language=en}}</ref>

One of Lippincott's earliest research contributions was the "Lippincott-Schroeder potential," a theoretical model for hydrogen bonding which he developed with his student Rudolph Schroeder.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lippincott |first1=Ellis R. |last2=Schroeder |first2=Rudolph |date=1957 |title=One-Dimensional Model of the Hydrogen Bond |doi=10.1063/1.1742196 |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=1099–1106}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lippincott |first1=Ellis R. |last2=Schroeder |first2=Rudolph |date=1959 |title=General Relation between Potential Energy and Internuclear Distance for Diatomic and Polyatomic Molecules. I |doi=10.1063/1.1742201 |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=1131–1141}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lippincott |first=Ellis R. |date=June 1957 |title=Derivation of an Internuclear Potential Function from a Quantum-Mechanical Model |doi=10.1063/1.1743605 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=1678–1685}}</ref> Of this work it has been said: "This fundamental research, cited almost 900 times as of February, 2024, describes the potential energy associated with the interaction between hydrogen atoms and an electronegative partner in a molecular complex. Despite being proposed in the 1950s, the LS potential has proven to be an enduring and accurate model for hydrogen bonds, remaining relevant even with the advent of sophisticated ab initio computations seven decades later. Multiple papers have been published evaluating and testing this model against experimental data, and it continues to stand as an accurate representation of the hydrogen bond, showcasing Lippincott's valuable contributions to chemistry."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Workman, Jr. |first=Jerome |date=June–July 2024 |title=Ellis Ridgeway Lippincott, A Legacy of Scientific Innovation |url=https://www.spectroscopyonline.com/view/ellis-ridgeway-lippincott-a-legacy-of-scientific-innovation |journal=Spectroscopy |volume=39 |issue=5 |pages=40–44}}</ref><ref>''See also'' Lippincott, Ellis R., Finch, Jack N., Schroeder, Rudolph, ''Potential Function Model of Hydrogen Bond Systems'', Papers Presented at the Symposium on Hydrogen Bonding Held at Ljubljana, 29 July–3 August 1957, 1959, pp. 361-374, https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-009140-2.50042-7.</ref>

Among other research, Lippincott investigated the organic evolution of living cells from non-living compounds (i.e., the origins of life) and studied the chemical composition of planetary atmospheres of [[Jupiter]], [[Mars]] and [[Venus]]. His research collaborators included [[Margaret Oakley Dayhoff]] and [[Carl Sagan]].<ref>{{Cite journal |first1=E. R. |last1=Lippincott |first2=M. O. |last2=Dayhoff |first3=Y. T. |last3=Pratt |date=August 5, 1966 |title=Thermodynamic equilibrium and the inorganic origin of organic compounds |url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.153.3736.628 |journal=Science |volume=153 |issue=3736 |pages=628–33|doi=10.1126/science.153.3736.628 |pmid=17757236 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>Dayhoff, M. O., E. R. Lippincott, R. V. Eck and G. Nagarajan. 1967. "Thermodynamic equilibrium in pre-biological atmospheres of C, H, O, N, P, S, and Cl." National Aeronautics and Space Administration Publication NASA SP-3040, Washington, D.C.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |first1=C. E. |last1=Sagan |first2=E. R. |last2=Lippincott |first3=M. O. |last3=Dayhoff |first4=R. V. |last4=Eck |date=January 21, 1967 |title=Organic Molecules and the Coloration of Jupiter |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/213273a0 |journal=Nature |volume=213 |issue=5073 |pages=273–274|doi=10.1038/213273a0 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lippincott |first1=Ellis R. |last2=Eck |first2=R. V. |last3=Dayhoff |first3=M. O. |last4=Sagan |first4=C. |date=1967 |title=Thermodynamic Equilibria in Planetary Atmospheres |url=https://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1967ApJ...147..753L |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=147 |pages=753–64 |doi=10.1086/149051 |bibcode=1967ApJ...147..753L |via=SAO/NASA Astrophysics Data System (ADS)}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dayhoff |first1=M. O. |last2=Eck |first2=R. |last3=Lippincott |first3=E. R. |last4=Sagan |first4=C. |date=February 3, 1967 |title=Venus: Atmospheric Evolution |journal=Science |volume=155 |issue=3762 |pages=556–558|doi=10.1126/science.155.3762.556 |pmid=17737405 }}</ref>

Lippincott was a consultant to the National Bureau of Standards. He served as an expert for the [[Food and Drug Administration]] in the investigation of the controversial cancer drug [[Krebiozen]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--Consulting |date=May 5, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-01-2 |edition=1st |location= |pages=110–165 |language=en}}</ref>

With two collaborators at the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|National Bureau of Standards]], Lippincott co-invented the [[Diamond anvil cell|Diamond Anvil High-Pressure Cell]], a device for investigating materials under pressure using [[diamond]]s which significantly increased the speed and accuracy of spectroscopic observations. The device was "one of the most valuable methods for making direct observations on the properties of a sample, a capability that had never before been possible."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bassett |first=William A. |date=2009-06-01 |title=Diamond anvil cell, 50th birthday |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/08957950802597239 |journal=High Pressure Research |publisher=Taylor & Francis |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=163–186 |doi=10.1080/08957950802597239 |issn=0895-7959|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Also with colleagues at the National Bureau of Standards, Lippincott was a lead investigator in the inquiry into anomalous water, also known as "[[polywater]]."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie |title=Polywater: An Inquiry into Anomalous Water |date=May 15, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-02-9 |edition=1st |language=en}}</ref>

== Publications ==
Lippincott was the author or co-author of over 160 peer-reviewed research papers and scientific articles published in such journals as ''Science, Nature, Journal of Physical Chemistry, Journal of Chemical Physics, Journal of the American Chemical Society, Journal of Research of the National Bureau of Standards, Journal of the Optical Society of America, Inorganic Chemistry, Analytical Chemistry, Applied Optics, Spectrochemica Acta'', and ''Journal of Chemical Education''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie L. |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--Publications |date=May 15, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-14-2 |pages=3–88 |language=en}}</ref> One of Lippincott's most impactful papers was his article entitled "The Limitations and Advantages of Infrared Spectroscopy in Patent Problems"<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lippincott |first=Ellis R. |date=1963 |title=The Limitations and Advantages of Infrared Spectroscopy in Patent Problems |journal=Journal of the Patent Office Society |volume=45 |issue=5 |pages=380–415}}</ref> published in the Journal of the Patent Office. As a result of his article, the Patent Office's view of infrared spectroscopy underwent a major change.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.optica.org/get_involved/awards_and_honors/awards/award_award_histories/lippincotthistory/#:~:text=Lippincott+presented+a+definitive+paper,Lippincott+died+in+1974.|title=Ellis R. Lippincott Award &#124; Optica|website=www.optica.org}}</ref>

== Scientific societies ==
Lippincott was a leading member of the community of scientists who worked in spectroscopy and related areas.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie L. |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--Professional Activities |date=May 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-08-1 |language=en}}</ref> His professional affiliations included the Optical Society of America (renamed Optica), Society for Applied Spectroscopy, Coblentz Society, [[American Chemical Society]], [[American Physical Society]], American Institute of Physics, Chemical Society of Washington, Philosophical Society of Washington, Washington Academy of Sciences, Society for Testing and Materials, [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]], [[Faraday Society]], and Chemical Society of London.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fein |first=Melanie L. |title=Ellis R. Lippincott Jr.--A Scientist in the Golden Age |date=May 15, 2024 |publisher=Partridge Press |isbn=978-1-963587-06-7 |pages=231–38 |language=en}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
Lippincott was a member of Phi Beta Kappa and other honorary societies. He was the 1964 recipient of the Chemical Society of Washington's Hillebrand Award and the 1970 recipient of the Pittsburgh Spectroscopy Award. The [[Ellis R. Lippincott Award]] was established in his honor in 1975 by the Optical Society (since renamed Optica), the Society for Applied Spectroscopy, and the Coblentz Society. The award is conferred annually on "an individual who has made significant contributions to vibrational spectroscopy as judged by their influence on other scientists" and "recognizes individuals whose work reflects the unique blend of theoretical insight, experimental proficiency, and transformative impact exemplified by Ellis R. Lippincott."<ref name="Spectroscopy 2024" /> Some of the world's most eminent spectroscopists have received this prestigious award during the past fifty years.{{efn|The first recipient of the award was Richard C. Lord, director of the Spectroscopy Laboratory at Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Other awardees are Lionel J. Bellamy, Bryce L. Crawford, George C. Pimentel, Peter R. Griffiths, and others.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.optica.org/get_involved/awards_and_honors/awards/award_descriptions/ellislippincott/|title=Ellis R. Lippincott Award &#124; Optica|website=www.optica.org}}</ref>}}

== Legacy ==
The trade magazine ''[[Spectroscopy (magazine)|Spectroscopy]]'' stated that "Lippincott's life is a testament to the power of scientific curiosity, innovation, and a commitment to reshaping perspectives, and looking at established 'truths' with an original and inquisitive perspective. His legacy lives on through the impact of his scientific methods and discoveries."<ref name="Spectroscopy 2024" />

== Personal life ==
Lippincott married Rita Clifton (1927–2024) in 1948, with whom he had five daughters. Ellis R. Lippincott Jr. died of Hodgkin's Disease in 1974 at the age of 54.{{Cn|date=September 2024}}<ref>Washington Post, Obituary Section, Ellis R. Lippincott, Jr., December 24, 1974.</ref>
